desc:
You are given a string s of lowercase letters. In one operation you may delete any occurrence of the substring 'ab' or of the substring 'cd'; the remaining parts then join together and can form new occurrences.

Return the smallest possible length of s after performing the operation as many times as you like.

Example: 'cabd' becomes 'cd' after deleting ab, and then the empty string, so the answer is 0. For 'acbbd' there is no 'ab' and no 'cd' at all, so the answer is 5.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: After a deletion, new occurrences of 'ab' or 'cd' can appear, so one pass with replace is not always enough.
A new character completes a deletable pair only together with the character directly before it in the already reduced text.
Keep a stack of survivors. When the current character is 'b' and the top is 'a', or the current character is 'd' and the top is 'c', pop instead of pushing. The final stack size is the answer.
editorial: Walk through the string and maintain the reduced text built so far as a stack. When a character arrives, the only pair it can complete is with the top of the stack: a followed by b, or c followed by d. If that happens we delete both by popping; otherwise we push the new character.

The two patterns share no letters, so a deletion of one kind never overlaps with the other kind, and the final reduced string is the same regardless of the order of deletions. That is why the greedy stack is optimal and the answer is simply its size. Time is O(n), extra space O(n).
